tables.how: Every passed Board file since 2014 that buys real property inside the city and whose title names the Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing or the State's Homekey program: 9 files, $370,000,000 in purchase prices, the case's $370.0 million. Seller and price are read from the file's title; each price was found printed in the title. Homes are the Budget Analyst's count of May 2024 where its audit lists the building, then the State's award list; 2 buildings (888 Post Street and 1174-1178 Folsom Street, 663 Clementina Street) have no count, so no price per home. The 7 with a count run from $224,000 to $725,000 a home; the case's lower figure of $200,000 is 333-7th Street, bought from Baker Places, Inc., which the next list counts as an existing residential building and not among these nine. The State award is the row of the State housing department's Homekey lists whose total equals the amount in the Board file that accepts a grant for the address (for 3055-3061 16th Street, the row whose capital amount the Budget Analyst prints for the building; the Board file's ceiling there is higher than the award listed). The award listed for 835 Turk Street is for building work after the purchase, not for the purchase itself. The appraiser and the reviewer are those the Budget Analyst's report on the purchase names; a blank means that report is not among the files collected. The escrow column adds the City's payments under the contracts titled as the building's acquisition.
tables.limits: A new apartment block and an old residential hotel are different goods, so a high price per home is a reason to read the appraisal, not a finding; the Budget Analyst's reports say each price they reviewed was confirmed by an appraisal and an appraisal review, and the appraisals themselves are not among the files collected. The State's list counts 170 homes at 333-12th Street where the count used here is 200. The State's list counts 51 homes at 5630-5638 Mission Street where the count used here is 52. The State's list counts 67 homes at 681-687 Ellis Street where the count used here is 74. The price per home uses the audit's count where there is one. A State award pays for operations as well as the purchase, and may be paid without passing through the escrow payments shown. The campaign-money column is the analysis's match on the seller's name only; none of the nine sellers was matched. A seller is named because the Board file names it; selling a building to the City at an appraised price is an ordinary transaction.

They add to $1,045,663,961, of which $326,690,953 is the whole cost of a new City office building at 1500-1580 Mission Street. Price per home is compared for the 9 finished buildings bought to house people whose number of homes is known (333-12th Street, 42 Otis Street, 1321 Mission Street, 5630-5638 Mission Street, 681-687 Ellis Street, 624 Laguna Street, 835 Turk Street, 3055-3061 16th Street, 333-7th Street): from $200,000 to $725,000, with a middle value of $268,919. 7 of those 9 are among the nine homeless-housing buildings of the first list; the others are 624 Laguna Street and 333-7th Street. Land bought under a new subsidized development shows the homes planned and is not compared.
tables.limits: Everything about a purchase is read from the title of its Board file, which gives the price, the seller and the address and not the appraisal, the condition or the negotiation. Where the City buys the land under a development it also lends to, the price is part of a financing plan and not a market purchase. An individual or a family trust is named where the Board file names it as the seller of a property to the City; that is a public transaction and not a finding. The campaign-money sentence is a match on a name only and is not confirmed.

tables.how: Every row of the four State lists that gives both homes and an award: 318 awards, 11 of them to San Francisco ($313,698,953 for 1,080 homes, $290,462 a home) and 307 elsewhere ($4,316,362,774 for 17,905 homes, $241,070 a home). Homekey Round 2: middle award per home $331,337 in San Francisco (4 of 116 awards) against $285,129 elsewhere. Homekey Round 3: middle award per home $307,376 in San Francisco (2 of 51 awards) against $286,992 elsewhere. Homekey+: middle award per home $326,255 in San Francisco (3 of 57 awards) against $361,989 elsewhere. Homekey Round 1: middle award per home $214,672 in San Francisco (2 of 94 awards) against $127,907 elsewhere. 9 of the 11 San Francisco awards are for buildings in this case (“1321 Mission” is 1321 Mission Street; “Eula Hotel Apartments” is 3055-3061 16th Street; “Mission Inn” is 5630-5638 Mission Street; “City Gardens” is 333-12th Street; “685 Ellis” is 681-687 Ellis Street; “42 Otis Street” is 42 Otis Street; “835 Turk Street” is 835 Turk Street; “Granada Hotel” is 1000 Sutter Street (Hotel Granada); “San Francisco: Homekey 2” is 440 Geary Street); the others are 1035 Van Ness and 629 Post. 19 rows of the lists give no homes or no award and are left out.
tables.limits: An award per home is what the State granted, not what a building cost: the City or a nonprofit pays the rest, and awards mix purchase money with operating subsidy in different proportions. Rounds had different rules and caps, and land and buildings cost more in San Francisco than in most of the State. Project names, uses and co-applicants in three of the lists were read from the layout of a PDF and can be misaligned; the award and home figures were checked against the lists' printed totals by the download step.

tables.how: The 43 purchases of the sale-history analysis: the 41 Board-approved purchases and the two hotels Episcopal Community Services bought (priced from the Budget Analyst's table). 41 could be matched to a lot; the rolls of 2007 to 2025 give an earlier sale date for 29 and a value re-set by that sale for 22; 8 are finished buildings that can be compared like for like. The prior sale falls within one year of the public purchase in 2 (681-687 Ellis Street; 1500-1580 Mission Street), within two in 5 (adding 888 Post Street; 1000 Sutter Street (Hotel Granada); 3300, 3306, and 3308 Mission Street) and within three in 8 (adding 2550 Irving Street; 4200 Geary Boulevard; 758 Pacific Avenue); 3 of the 8 are comparable like for like (681-687 Ellis Street (295 days, +39%); 888 Post Street (727 days, +190%); 1000 Sutter Street (Hotel Granada) (477 days, +53%)). 3 more fall between three and four years (5630-5638 Mission Street; 333-12th Street; 1515 South Van Ness Avenue). 12 matched purchases show no earlier sale date; for 3 of them the land value was re-set in some year without one (1174-1178 Folsom Street, 663 Clementina Street; 2280 Market Street; 240-6th Street). In 4 purchases the price was below the assessed value on the last roll before (440 Geary Street; 1036 Mission Street; 1660 and 1670 Mission Street; 2280 Market Street). The public purchase is dated by the day the Board file was introduced; for the two hotels, by the sale date the roll records. The value columns and the comparison are those the analysis computed; the prior sale date was re-read from the rolls for this list and agrees for every row.
tables.limits: The assessor's roll records no price and names no owner. It gives one sale date for a lot each year and the assessed value of the land and the building; California law re-sets that value to the price paid when a property changes hands, so the value that appears after a sale date indicates the price and no more: an exemption, a transfer of part of a property, a transfer the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break the link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder name the parties and settle the price; neither is published as data, so no earlier buyer or seller is named here. That the seller to the City is the party that bought on the earlier sale date is an inference from there being no sale date in between. A higher price a few years on has ordinary causes: a developer who finished a building, a seller who renovated or emptied it, a market that rose, a first sale at a distressed price, or furniture, a business or a lease sold with a hotel. Where the City buys the land under a subsidized development from the partnership it lends to, a recent sale date is how the financing is built. The City was already paying for rooms in the hotel at 681-687 Ellis Street before it bought it: contract 1000022511 with 685 Ellis LLC, titled “HSA0590 COVID19 Hotel Rooms”, has a term from 2020-05-26 and $4,775,600 paid, printed under fiscal 2022 and 2023; the roll's earlier sale date there is 2021-06-14.

tables.how: For the lots of each of the 43 purchases (and the lots they were split from or merged into), every roll year from 2007 to 2025 was read and each distinct sale date listed: 55 dates. The value a sale set is land plus building on the first later roll where the land value moves by more than the yearly inflation factor, looked for up to four rolls after the date. A date on or after the public purchase and within two years of it is read as the roll's own record of that purchase. Purchases with no sale date, or with no lot matched, have one row saying so.
tables.limits: The assessor's roll records no price and names no owner. It gives one sale date for a lot each year and the assessed value of the land and the building; California law re-sets that value to the price paid when a property changes hands, so the value that appears after a sale date indicates the price and no more: an exemption, a transfer of part of a property, a transfer the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break the link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder name the parties and settle the price; neither is published as data, so no earlier buyer or seller is named here. The seller named on a row is the party that sold to the City or to the nonprofit in the public purchase, as the Board file names it; the rolls do not say who bought or sold on any earlier date. Sale dates are thinly kept on the 2017 roll and from 2020 on, so an absent date is not an absent sale.

For the two sites the audit re-checked, 835 Turk Street and 1000 Sutter Street, repair estimates rose from $15,602,150 to $85,309,595, $69,707,445 more. The repair column of Exhibit 3.3 adds to $113,133,355 over its rows as printed, while its total line prints $121,921,205: the difference, $8,787,850, is the rise at 835 Turk Street, whose row prints the first estimate. The row for 1000 Sutter Street already prints the revised figure. 6 of the eight were bought by the City and are in the first list; 440 Geary Street and 1000 Sutter Street were bought by Episcopal Community Services with a State grant and City money. 3 of the City's nine purchases (42 Otis Street, 888 Post Street, 1174-1178 Folsom Street, 663 Clementina Street) are not in the audit's table.
tables.limits: These are the auditor's figures as of May 2024, not final costs. The audit faults the estimates, not the sellers or the operators, and says unforeseen conditions are always possible in old buildings; it reports that inspections before purchase covered immediate repair needs and accessibility and not building systems, hazardous materials or ground conditions. The next list gives the later figures the Budget Analyst reported to the Board for the same buildings.

tables.how: For every Board file of the list above whose Budget Analyst report was collected, each table titled as an acquisition, rehabilitation, renovation, capital, development or total-cost budget was read line by line, from its title to its source line: 137 lines from 17 reports. Where a table prints an earlier plan beside the proposed one, the proposed amount is the amount and the earlier one is shown beside it; one report that covers two files is listed once. Read in date order for one building, the lines show how the repair figure moved: at 1000 Sutter Street, rehabilitation of $6,540,000 in September 2020, $18,717,610 in November 2020 and construction of $53,651,042 with soft costs of $10,318,401 in July 2024; at 835 Turk Street, an improvement cost of $9,062,150 in January 2022, building rehabilitation of $17,850,000 in December 2022 and hard costs of $20,275,720 with soft costs of $8,187,121 in December 2025.
tables.limits: The lines are budgets and estimates put before the Board, not payments. They were read by rule from the text of each report: a label that wraps, a footnote mark or a column of changes can be misread, and the link opens the report, which governs. Reports that were not collected (among them those on the purchases of 888 Post Street, 1174-1178 Folsom Street and 42 Otis Street and on the 440 Geary loan) leave no rows. A rise in a repair budget is not a finding against a seller or an operator: the Budget Analyst attributes the rises to conditions found after purchase, seismic work and a change of plan.

tables.how: The contracts of the list above that are titled as construction or rehabilitation, or that are agreements of the Mayor's housing office with a building's owner or its lender: 17 contracts, agreed at $159,475,462 with $141,329,079 paid. They include the $48,000,000 agreed with the San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund on 1000 Sutter Street ($44,386,912 paid) and the $16,738,663 agreed with 1000 Sutter LLC on the same day (Board file 240730 buys the Fund's loan and sets the City's loan at up to $71,125,575), the $47,386,810 loan to 440 Geary LLC (Board file 230927, up to $47,390,000), the $13,000,000 agreed with 685 Ellis Housing Partners from 2025-12-19, the $5,364,750 of work at 888 Post Street from 2020-03-30, while the City was still the tenant, and the $1,517,444 for site repairs at 1178 Folsom Street.
tables.limits: The contract table does not say what a loan or grant to an owner pays for: several of the smaller yearly agreements with 1000 Sutter LLC and 440 Geary LLC are operating subsidies, not building work, and the 440 Geary loan is described in its Board file as permanent financing, which repays the purchase money as well as the work. No City construction contract was found for the buildings the City owns and leases to an operator, because the operator or a nonprofit owner hires the builder; the builders are therefore not in City data. The amounts are ceilings and payments, not the repair bill, which is in the Budget Analyst's tables.

A building is tied to a contract or payment by the address in the title, or by a name that a record ties to the address: “City Gardens” (the State's award list gives that name to the award of $56,578,000 that Board file 221170 accepts for 333-12th Street, and the seller is City Gardens Bridge, LLC); “Margot” (the ordinance in Board file 220874 names 1321 Mission Street for Margot Antonetty); “Mission Inn” (the Budget Analyst's report on Board file 210941); “Eula” and “Casa Esperanza” (the State award to “Eula Hotel Apartments” has the capital amount, $5,763,280, that the Budget Analyst prints for 3061 16th Street; contract 1000024908 is titled “Larkin - Eula Hotel SS” in the earlier years of the payment table and “Larkin - SS at Casa Esperanza” later; and contract 1000027872, “Dolores - Casa Esperanza ML”, is agreed at the $7,147,000 of Board file 221157 for 3055-3061 16th Street); “Granada” and “Hotel Diva” (Board files 201063 and 201193 and the Budget Analyst's reports on them); “SOMA TAY” (contract 1000033445 is agreed at the $14,177,264 of Board file 240848 for 1174-1178 Folsom Street); and “TAY Nav” (Board file 260795 names 3rd Street Youth Center and Clinic as the tenant running a navigation center for young adults at 888 Post Street; no number ties that contract to the address, so it is not confirmed). A payee that exists for one building only (1000 Sutter LLC, 440 Geary LLC, 685 Ellis LLC, 685 Ellis Housing Partners, City Gardens Bridge LLC) is tied by its name. What a contract is for is read from its title: a payment to a title company or titled “acquisition” is purchase money; “ML” is a lease and property management agreement; “PM” property management; “SS” support services. A Board file is linked where the contract's agreed amount equals an amount in that file's title for the same building.
tables.limits: The table shows a contract's present amount and keeps no history. A contract of the Mayor's housing office with a building's owner can be a loan for building work, a yearly operating subsidy or both; the title does not say which. Each organization's payments in the two tables the Controller publishes, as retrieved on 12 November 2026: Citywide Nonprofit Spending, which by its own description keeps contracted services only, and Vendor Payments (Vouchers), the table of every payment. The fiscal year is the one printed on the payment. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use: the name without punctuation and company suffixes, plus the renames and spellings that a shared contract number confirms.
tables.limits: These are each organization's whole City payments, most of them for other buildings and programs: the payment list above gives the part paid under the contracts for these buildings. An organization that manages a building passes most of what it is paid on to staff, utilities and repairs. A payment is money the City sent, not money the organization kept or spent on itself: subsidies, rent aid and grants that an organization pays on to others are in these figures. The two tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table leaves out a kind of payment or a contract; neither is wrong for that reason. The year printed on a payment can be later than the year the payment was issued. A payee the City spells in a way that no contract number ties to the organization is not counted.

tables.how: Every passed Board file since 2014 whose title has the City as tenant, less terminations and assignments: 126 files, of which 122 could be matched to a lot, at 78 sites; the rolls give an earlier sale date for 72. 7 new leases were introduced within two years after the building's last sale date (945 Bryant Street, 162 days; 888 Post Street, 195 days; 1360 Mission Street, 256 days; 250 Kearny Street, 371 days; 258A Laguna Honda Boulevard, 475 days; 2000 Oakdale Avenue, 508 days; 752 Vallejo Street, 628 days); 2 buildings changed hands again within two years after a new City lease (945 Bryant Street, sale dated 2019-05-01; 1076 Howard Street, sale dated 2022-07-18); at 2 sites a sale date falls between the first and the last lease file. Files at the same lots are read as one tenancy. The first-year rent is shown only for the 60 leases whose rent the property analysis kept in its output; flagged files are listed first.
tables.limits: A landlord buying a building with a tenant in view, or with the City already in it, is ordinary commercial practice, and a long lease to a government tenant makes a building worth more to the next buyer. City leases are negotiated, not bid, and above a set rent the law requires an appraisal that is not in these files. Board files start in 2014, so a first file on record may renew a much older lease. The assessor's roll records no price and names no owner. It gives one sale date for a lot each year and the assessed value of the land and the building; California law re-sets that value to the price paid when a property changes hands, so the value that appears after a sale date indicates the price and no more: an exemption, a transfer of part of a property, a transfer the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break the link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder name the parties and settle the price; neither is published as data, so no earlier buyer or seller is named here. That the landlord named in the file bought on the earlier sale date is an inference. An individual or a family trust is named where the Board file names it as the City's landlord.

tables.how: Every line of the lists of business dealings with insiders on the returns collected (latest version of each, tax years 2020 to 2025) whose description contains rent, rental, lease, landlord or tenant: 45 lines from 9 organizations. One amount is counted for an organization, an insider and a year; an organization whose returns spell its name two ways is listed under the name on its latest return, its employer identification number being the tie. 6 organizations report an arrangement in which they are not described as the landlord, $956,301 in all: Union Square Business Improvement District dba Union Square Alliance $378,125; 18 Reasons $187,245; Union Square Foundation $169,016; Mid-Market Foundation $140,500; Transgender Advocates for Justice and Accountability Coalition $43,415; The Unity Care Group $38,000. 2 organizations collect rent from insiders, $4,060,378: San Francisco Market Corporation and UCSF Health Community Hospitals Fka Saint Francis Memorial Hospital (a wholesale market whose merchant tenants sit on its board, and a hospital renting to its doctors, as the case words it). First Voice Inc reports rent with insiders on 4 returns and gives no amount, so it is in neither figure.
tables.limits: Reporting the arrangement is what the law requires, and a board member who rents space to a charity at or below market does it a favour. The returns do not say whether the rent is at market, which building is rented, or whether City money pays it; where the return does not say which way the rent goes, it is not known that the organization is the one paying. Every person listed is described on the return itself as a board member, a director, an officer or a founder, present or former, or as a broker with an ownership interest in the building. None of this is about the buildings the City bought: no seller or operator of those buildings is on this list. A tax return is the organization's own statement, signed under penalty of perjury and not audited by the IRS. Its tax year is often not the City's fiscal year, and it counts money when earned or spent under its accounting method, not when the City paid. A disclosure on a return, including a dealing with an officer or a director, is what the law requires to be reported; the question is whether it is fair and approved.

tables.limits: A related organization is one the filer controls or is controlled by: a nonprofit that holds its building in a separate company, a hospital and its medical foundation. Such leases are routine and the return is where they are meant to be reported. The amount is the year's rent or lease payments as reported, not City money. A tax return is the organization's own statement, signed under penalty of perjury and not audited by the IRS. Its tax year is often not the City's fiscal year, and it counts money when earned or spent under its accounting method, not when the City paid. A disclosure on a return, including a dealing with an officer or a director, is what the law requires to be reported; the question is whether it is fair and approved.

tables.limits: City paid is everything the City paid the organization, not the rent, and the returns do not say that City money pays the rent. A business improvement district is paid the assessments the City collects for it from property owners. A payment is money the City sent, not money the organization kept or spent on itself: subsidies, rent aid and grants that an organization pays on to others are in these figures. The two tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table leaves out a kind of payment or a contract; neither is wrong for that reason.
